strengths: First successful framework for joint training of LAM with pretrained video-generation-based world models, solving a previously unaddressed problem
Rigorous empirical diagnosis of the collapse phenomenon with systematic analysis of different initialization schemes and codebook metrics
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets, metrics, and downstream tasks with thorough ablations demonstrating synergistic co-evolution
Insightful analysis of codebook dynamics during adaptation (Section D.1) that reveals latent action robustness differences missed by linear probing
Well-motivated warm-up solution that effectively aligns representations and enables stable joint training
Practical benefits demonstrated in downstream adaptation, particularly showing robustness to imperfect action adapters
weaknesses: Limited theoretical understanding of the fundamental collapse mechanism—the hypothesis that pretrained models cause misalignment is intuitive but not rigorously analyzed
Warm-up solution is engineering-focused rather than principled; alternative alignment strategies unexplored, and hyperparameter selection (8K steps) lacks principled justification

Linear probing results contradict central LAM quality claims (Table 5 shows joint training sometimes performs worse), and the post-hoc explanation that linear probing 'captures only one aspect' weakens the argument
Efficiency gains are overstated: joint training has higher per-step cost (6s vs. 3.6-5.5s), and total time savings are marginal (~12 hours on ~75 hour baseline, within experimental variance)
Improvements in most metrics are marginal (PSNR <1%, LPIPS within noise), with substantial gains only on FVD; practical significance of perceptual metric improvements unclear
Weak performance on complex control tasks (21.2% success on tractable RoboDesk tasks) limits evidence for practical utility of improvements
Limited baseline comparisons—primarily 2-stage approach; AC-LAM and MVP-LAM mentioned but not compared quantitatively; AdaWorld only on visual planning
Generalizability concerns: method tightly coupled to OpenSora with limited evaluation on alternative backbones (only Wan2.1); unclear how broadly approach applies
Substantial computational requirements (8 H200 GPUs, 100 hours) and no code release mentioned, limiting reproducibility
Missing ablations on alternatives (freezing IDM instead of WM, gradual unfreezing, other alignment strategies) leave solution space underexplored

strengths: Clear problem motivation: Identifies redundancy in two-stage pipeline where FDM and world model both predict next frames
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple datasets (OXE, EgoCentric, AgiBot, LIBERO) with standard metrics and ablations
Systematic empirical documentation of VQ codebook collapse and systematic investigation through different initialization conditions (Figure 2)
Strong analysis of downstream real-action adaptation showing codebook robustness (Figure 5), revealing value beyond raw video metrics
Well-structured presentation with clear visualizations demonstrating synergistic co-evolution mechanism (Figure 4)
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Core contribution is replacing FDM with world model plus adding warm-up phase; AdaLN conditioning borrowed from prior work
Insufficient mechanistic understanding: Paper identifies misalignment as the cause but doesn't explain why freezing the world model resolves it or why random IDM + random WM doesn't collapse
Marginal improvements on primary metrics: FVD improvements in Table 1 are modest (289.37→278.90 on OXE), linear probing differences negligible (0.1614 vs 0.1623 on LIBERO)
Misleading computational efficiency claims: Comparing different training budgets (WARM8K+E2E30K vs LAM30K+WM30K) and omitting that per-step costs are higher for joint training (6s vs 5.5s)
Experimental design issues: 2-stage baseline uses LAM30K but comparison to LAM8K (equivalent warm-up length) missing; no error bars or significance tests despite small improvements
Lack of statistical rigor: Visual planning results use only 5 seeds without confidence intervals; unclear if differences like 21.20% vs 7.73% are statistically significant
Narrow scope: Evaluation limited to robotic manipulation; alternate backbone (Wan2.1) relegated to appendix; low absolute success rates on complex tasks (Table 3) for all methods
Missing analysis of warm-up mechanism: No principled criterion for selecting warm-up duration (8K chosen empirically); unclear why codebook collapse is specific to pretrained+random initialization

strengths: Clear problem identification: Systematically demonstrates why naive joint training fails (Figure 2) through codebook collapse metrics, with well-motivated critique of two-stage redundancy
Comprehensive empirical validation: Multiple datasets, metrics, and proper ablations showing bidirectional co-evolution benefits both components (Figure 4)

Strong downstream performance: Significant improvements in real-action adaptation (FVD: 115.45→93.68 on LIBERO) and visual planning (7.73%→21.20% on RoboDesk benchmark), demonstrating practical utility
Mechanistic insights: D.1's codebook analysis elegantly explains why 2-stage methods suffer catastrophic collapse during adaptation while co-evolution preserves diversity
Data efficiency: Achieves comparable performance to 2-stage baseline in less wall-clock time (~63h vs ~75h) while providing superior generalization
Model-agnostic paradigm: Validated on multiple video generation backbones (OpenSora, Wan2.1), demonstrating broad applicability
Scalability evidence: Shows consistent improvements with larger models (D.3) and different batch sizes (D.6), supporting the approach's robustness
weaknesses: Limited theoretical justification: Why initialization misalignment causes VQ codebook collapse is explained intuitively but lacks rigorous analysis; warm-up strategy is empirically effective but feels like a pragmatic patch

Warm-up design lacks principles: Selection of 8K steps appears arbitrary; no principled method for determining warm-up duration provided; different models require different durations without clear guidance
Modest pixel-level improvements: PSNR gains <0.5 across most datasets; SSIM improvements ~0.2-0.3; LPIPS changes within noise margins, raising questions about practical significance of some metrics

Negligible linear probing differences: Table 5 shows marginal or sometimes worse probing loss despite better world model controllability, which undermines claims about LAM quality independent of world model coupling

Computational overhead not fully addressed: Per-step cost higher (~6s vs 5.5s); while end-to-end training is competitive, the per-step overhead is presented minimally and involves trade-offs with 2-stage FDM efficiency

Narrow experimental scope: Limited to robotic manipulation; unclear if results generalize to other domains (discrete action spaces, visual games); all datasets are relatively controlled manipulation scenarios
Low absolute performance on complex tasks: Visual planning success rates remain modest; performance degrades significantly on precise manipulation tasks, limiting claims about practical applicability

Statistical rigor lacking: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars reported; most experiments appear to be single runs, making it difficult to assess result reliability for modest improvements
